seq.body:
Searching is the thing programs do most, and the simplest method is the one you would use without thinking. Searching is the most common operation a program performs: find a student by roll number, a word in a dictionary, a customer by account. Given a collection of records and a key, return the record with that key or report that none exists. The method depends on how the data is organised, and the cost is measured by counting key comparisons — the same unit we used for sorting.

The baseline is sequential (linear) search: examine records one by one from the start until the key is found or the data runs out. It needs no preparation and works on arrays and linked lists, sorted or not. For n records a successful search takes 1 comparison at best, n at worst, and (n + 1)/2 on average if every position is equally likely; an unsuccessful search always takes n. It is O(n). A small speed-up is the sentinel: put a copy of the key after the last element so the loop need not test for the end of the array on every pass. On a sorted array an unsuccessful search can stop as soon as it meets a larger key — saving half the comparisons on average, but it is still O(n). For tiny collections, or one-off searches in unsorted data, sequential search is exactly right; for repeated searches in large collections we need something smarter.

What is the average number of comparisons when the key is equally likely to be anywhere in an array of n items?
keynotes: Given a collection of records and a key, search returns the record with that key or reports that none exists, and cost is counted in key comparisons.
Sequential (linear) search examines records one by one from the start until the key is found or the data runs out.
It needs no preparation and works on any data, with average (n + 1)/2 comparisons and worst case n.

bs.body:
When you look for “mango” in a dictionary you do not start at A, and that habit is exactly binary search. Open a dictionary to find “mango”. You do not start at A: you open near the middle, see that you are at “L”, so you know the word is in the second half, and halve again. Binary search does exactly that on a sorted array: compare the key with the middle element; if equal, done; if the key is smaller, discard the upper half; if larger, discard the lower half; repeat on what remains until the range is empty. Each comparison halves the candidates, so the number of probes is at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1: one million sorted items need at most 20 probes, a billion at most 30. The price is the requirement of sorted data with random access — it does not work on a linked list (no O(1) middle) or an unsorted array — and the cost of keeping the data sorted when it changes.

The code is a loop with two indices, lo and hi, and mid = (lo + hi) / 2 (to avoid overflow on huge arrays write lo + (hi − lo)/2). Take care with the boundaries: it is the single most commonly mis-coded algorithm. The program searches 53 in a ten-element array — three probes — and then the absent key 10, which takes three probes before the range empties. The recursive version, which passes lo and hi as parameters, has the recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 from Chapter 1: O(log n).

How many probes does a sorted array of a million items need at most? Work it out from ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1.
keynotes: Binary search compares the key with the middle element and discards the upper or lower half, repeating on what remains.
Each comparison halves the candidates, so the number of probes is at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1.
It needs sorted, random-access data.

hashidea.body:
Binary search gives O(log n); could we do better still? Here is the idea that gets you to O(1). Binary search finds a key in O(log n). Can we find it in O(1)? If the keys were small integers we could use the key itself as the array index — direct addressing: the record for roll number 305 is stored at table[305]. Search, insert and delete are then a single array access. The trouble is the size of the key space. Student numbers might run from 0 to 99,999,999 for a class of 60; reserving 100 million slots to hold 60 records is absurd, and names or phone numbers are not even integers.

Hashing keeps the speed and shrinks the table. Choose a table of m slots, much smaller than the key space, and a hash function h that maps any key to an index in 0…m − 1. Store the record at table[h(key)]; to look it up, compute h(key) again and go straight there. Search, insert and delete are O(1) on average. The catch is unavoidable: if there are more possible keys than slots, two different keys must sometimes map to the same slot — a collision — and every hash table needs a strategy to resolve them. The table of m slots holding n keys has a load factor α = n/m; the whole performance story depends on keeping α moderate.

Why can we not simply use a phone number as an array index? Think how large the array would have to be.
keynotes: Direct addressing stores the record for key 305 at table[305], so search, insert and delete are a single array access.
The trouble is the size of the key space: reserving 100 million slots to hold 60 records is absurd, and names are not even integers.
Hashing keeps the speed of direct addressing but squeezes the key space into a small table with a hash function.

hfn.body:
A hash function is the heart of the idea, and you can judge a good one by three simple tests. You will see that the recipes differ in cleverness but all share one aim, which is to make keys that look alike land far apart. A good hash function is fast to compute, always returns the same value for the same key, and spreads typical keys uniformly across the table, so each slot is equally likely to be chosen. Several classic recipes exist. The division method uses h(k) = k mod m: simple and fast, but m must be chosen carefully — a power of 2 (which just keeps the low bits) or a number sharing factors with the key patterns gives poor spread, so a prime not close to a power of 2 is the usual choice. The multiplication method takes the fractional part of k·A (A ≈ 0.618, the golden ratio fraction) and scales it by m; it works with any m. The mid-square method squares the key and takes the middle digits: 1234² = 1,522,756, whose middle two digits are 27. Folding splits the key into parts and adds them: 123 456 78 → 123 + 456 + 78 = 657, then mod 100 gives 57.

For strings, treat the characters as digits of a number in some base and reduce modulo m as you go — polynomial hashing: h = (h·31 + c) mod m for each character c. For the string “cab” with a = 1, b = 2, c = 3 this gives 3, then 3·31 + 1 = 94, then 94·31 + 2 = 2916 ≡ 88 (mod 101). The factor 31 (or another prime) ensures that “ab” and “ba” hash differently. Never use the sum of the character codes alone: anagrams would all collide. Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) are far slower and are used for integrity and passwords, not for table lookups.

Why is a table size of 64 a poor choice for the division method, and a prime such as 61 a better one? Then hash the keys 12, 25, 38 and 51 by hand with m = 13 and look at what happens.
keynotes: A good hash function is fast, deterministic and spreads typical keys uniformly across the table.
The division method uses h(k) = k mod m with m a prime not close to a power of 2.
The multiplication method takes the fractional part of k times a constant; other recipes are mid-square, folding and polynomial hashing for strings.

coll.body:
Two different keys will sometimes land in the same slot, and you can cure it simply by letting a slot hold more than one key. The simplest remedy is to let a slot hold more than one key. In separate chaining each slot of the table is the head of a linked list; to insert, compute h(k) and add the key to that list (at the front, O(1)); to search, compute h(k) and scan only that list; to delete, remove the node from the list. The table never “fills”: chains just grow. With n keys in m slots the average chain has length α = n/m, so an unsuccessful search costs about 1 + α probes (one for the slot, α for the chain) and a successful one about 1 + α/2. Keep α near 1 or below and every operation is O(1) on average. The weakness is extra memory for the pointers and poorer cache behaviour; chains can be kept sorted or replaced by balanced trees (Java’s HashMap does this for long chains) to bound the worst case.

Insert 5, 10, 3, 8 into five slots with h(k) = k mod 5: 5 and 10 both hash to slot 0 and 3 and 8 to slot 3, giving the table 5|10 - - 3|8 - — two chains of length two, four probes in total. The card shows the chains growing.

With 100 keys in 50 slots what is the average chain length α, and how many probes does an unsuccessful search cost?
keynotes: In separate chaining each slot is the head of a linked list: insert adds to the list, search scans only that list.
The table never fills; chains just grow, and with n keys in m slots the average chain length is α = n/m.
An unsuccessful search costs about 1 + α probes.

open.body:
The other family keeps everything inside the array, so when a slot is taken you simply try another according to a fixed rule. The price is that you must be careful, because the way you leave and re-enter a slot affects every later search for any key. The other family keeps everything inside the table array, with no pointers. In open addressing, if the home slot h(k) is occupied, probe a fixed sequence of other slots until a free one is found. To search, follow the same sequence until you find the key or reach an empty slot (meaning it is absent). The table can hold at most m keys and must stay well below full. The probe sequence defines the scheme. In linear probing the i-th probe is (h(k) + i) mod m — try the next slot, then the next. It is simple and cache-friendly, but suffers primary clustering: runs of occupied slots grow, and any key hashing into a run extends it, so probe lengths balloon. Quadratic probing uses (h(k) + i²) mod m, jumping 1, 4, 9 slots away; it breaks up primary clusters but keys with the same home slot still share a probe sequence (secondary clustering), and for guaranteed success the table size should be prime and the load below ½. Double hashing uses a second hash for the step, (h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) mod m, so different keys with the same home slot follow different sequences; with h₂ never 0 (for instance 1 + k mod (m − 1)) and m prime it comes closest to the ideal of uniform probing.

Insert 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101 into seven slots, h = k mod 7. Linear probing gives 700 50 85 92 73 101 76 using 13 probes in total; quadratic gives 700 50 85 73 101 92 76 (11 probes); double hashing gives 700 50 101 85 92 73 76 (11 probes). The first keys fall in their home slots (50 → 1, 700 → 0, 85 → 1…), then collide: 85 finds slot 1 taken by 50 and moves on. Step through the cards and watch the probe sequences — red slots were probed and found occupied. The first program reproduces the linear-probing table, including 13 probes.

Deletion needs care. If you simply empty a slot, you may cut a probe sequence in the middle: a later search for a key stored beyond it would stop at the hole and wrongly report “absent”. The standard fix is a tombstone: mark the slot “deleted”; searches continue past it, and insertions may reuse it. Too many tombstones degrade performance and trigger a rehash.

Why must deletion in open addressing leave a marker, a tombstone, and not simply empty the slot? Then insert three colliding keys with linear probing and notice how the occupied slots grow into a block.
keynotes: In open addressing, if the home slot h(k) is occupied we probe a fixed sequence of other slots until a free one is found.
Linear probing tries (h(k) + i) mod m, simple and cache-friendly but prone to clustering.
The table can hold at most m keys and must stay well below full.

perf.body:
How much does all this cost? The answer depends on a single number, the load factor, and you can compute it. How much does collision resolution cost? Under the usual assumption of uniform hashing the expected number of probes depends only on the load factor α. With chaining: 1 + α for an unsuccessful search and 1 + α/2 for a successful one. With linear probing the classic results (Knuth) are about ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)²) probes for an unsuccessful search and ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)) for a successful one; uniform probing (the ideal that double hashing approaches) gives 1/(1 − α) and (1/α) ln(1/(1 − α)). The table shows how sharply open addressing degrades as the table fills: at α = 0.5 an unsuccessful linear-probing search costs 2.5 probes, at 0.8 it costs 13, at 0.9 it costs 50.5.

The practical rules follow directly. Keep α below about 0.5–0.7 for open addressing and below about 1–2 for chaining. When the load exceeds the threshold, rehash: allocate a larger table (about double, then the next prime), and re-insert every key with the new hash function, since the index depends on m. A single rehash costs O(n), but as with the doubling array it is amortised: inserting n keys costs O(n) in total, so each insertion is O(1) amortised.

Compute the expected probes for chaining and linear probing at α = 0.5 and α = 0.9 and compare. Notice how sharply open addressing degrades.
keynotes: With chaining the expected probes are 1 + α for an unsuccessful search and 1 + α/2 for a successful one.
With linear probing they are about ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)²) and ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)); uniform probing gives 1/(1 − α) and (1/α) ln(1/(1 − α)).
Open addressing degrades sharply as the load factor approaches 1, so tables are rehashed to a larger size.

use.body:
Hash tables are the workhorse of everyday programming, and you have almost certainly used one without noticing. Hash tables are the workhorse of everyday programming: dictionaries and sets (C++ unordered_map and unordered_set, Python dict, Java HashMap), symbol tables in compilers, caches, database hash indexes and hash joins, de-duplication, counting frequencies, and memoisation tables. Related uses of hash functions include checksums, the Rabin–Karp string-matching algorithm, Bloom filters (a compact probabilistic “probably present” test) and password storage with a salted cryptographic hash. The program counts word frequencies — the classic hash-table job.

But hashing scatters keys, so it keeps no order. Finding the smallest key, the next larger key, or all keys in a range is O(n) on a hash table; a balanced tree or B-tree answers those in O(log n) and lists the results in sorted order. If you need only exact-match lookup, use a hash table; if you need order or range queries, use a tree. Worst-case guarantees also differ: a hash table can degrade to O(n) with bad luck or an adversary choosing colliding keys (defended by randomised hash functions), while a balanced tree is O(log n) always. Perfect hashing for a fixed key set and cuckoo hashing (two tables, each key has two possible homes) give O(1) worst-case lookups.

Name three places in programs you have written where a dictionary or set would have been the right tool.
keynotes: Dictionaries and sets (unordered_map, Python dict, Java HashMap), compiler symbol tables, caches, database hash indexes, de-duplication and frequency counting all use hash tables.
Related uses are checksums, Rabin–Karp string matching, Bloom filters and password storage with a salted cryptographic hash.
Hashing does not keep keys in order, so it is the wrong tool for range queries.

summary.body:
Let’s finish with a short list so you can check what you now know about searching.

  • Sequential search: O(n), any data; average (n + 1)/2. Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted random-access data; at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes.
  • Hashing maps keys to slots with h(k); load factor α = n/m; collisions are unavoidable.
  • Good hash functions spread keys evenly: division (prime m), multiplication, mid-square, folding, polynomial for strings.
  • Chaining: lists per slot, expected 1 + α probes. Open addressing: linear (clusters), quadratic, double hashing; deletion needs tombstones.
  • Open addressing degrades sharply with α, so rehash (double and re-insert) around 0.5–0.7; amortised O(1) per insertion.
  • Hash tables give O(1) exact lookup but no order; use trees for range and sorted queries.

For each method, say its cost and what it needs from the data. If you hesitate, revisit that section.
keynotes: Sequential search is O(n) on any data; binary search is O(log n) and needs sorted random-access data.
Hashing maps keys to slots with h(k); load factor α = n/m and collisions are unavoidable.
Chaining gives expected 1 + α probes; open addressing uses linear, quadratic or double hashing and deletion needs tombstones.
